       COMMISSION STAFF’S EXCEPTIONS TO THE PROPOSAL FOR DECISION

                                                  I.         INTRODUCTION

          The (Staff) of the Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission) respectfully files

these exceptions to the proposal for decision (PFD) filed by the administrative law judges (ALJs)

from the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH) on August 20, 2026, on the applications

of Oncor Electric Delivery Company, LLC (Oncor) and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation

(LCRA TSC) (collectively, the Applicants) to amend their certificates of convenience and

necessity (CCN) for (1) the proposed Bell County East-to-Big Hill 765-kilovolt (kV) transmission

line project and, (2) on need only, the proposed Big Hill-to-Sand Lake 765-kV transmission line

project. Pursuant to the Exceptions and Replies Memorandum filed on August 20, 2026, these

exceptions are timely filed.

          Staff respectfully disagrees with the PFD’s findings on notice, need, and routing. On notice,

the PFD concludes that the Applicants failed to comply with the notice requirements under 16

Texas Administrative Code (TAC) § 22.52(a)(3) and (4) based on flawed and impractical rule

interpretations. On the need for the projects that together comprise Import Path 2, the PFD fails to

the proposed 765-kV transmission line projects for Import Path 2 are needed for system reliability.

       II.        EXCEPTIONS TO FINDINGS OF NONCOMPLIANCE WITH NOTICE

                                                       REQUIREMENTS

          Staff disagrees with the PFD’s recommendations that the Applicants failed to meet the

notice requirements of 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(3) and (a)(4) because the record and Commission

precedent demonstrate that the Applicants satisfied those requirements. The PFD argues that the

Applicants are required by 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(3) to use current county tax rolls at the time of the

filing of the application to provide notice.2 That is a novel and unprecedented interpretation of the

Commission’s notice rule. In addition, the PFD concludes that the Applicants were required to

hold additional public meetings to comply with 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4),3 despite Commission

precedent to the contrary. Staff disagrees with both conclusions and respectfully contends that the

Applicants sufficiently satisfied both 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(3) and (a)(4).

           Notice of the Application under 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(3)

          Under 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(3), an applicant must “on the date it files an application, mail

notice of its application to the owners of land, as stated on the current county tax rolls, who would

be directly affected by the requested certificate.” It is not explicitly clear what “current county tax

rolls”4 means. However, the PFD incorrectly concludes that the rule requires the use of county tax

rolls that are current as of the date the application is filed.5

          PURA § 37.054 requires notice of an application on filing but does not specify the source

of information applicants must rely on to identify landowners for notice purposes. Additionally,

the section does not prescribe how current the information must be.6 While 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(3)

requires that applicants rely on “current county tax rolls” to identify landowners for notice

purposes, the text and structure of the rule do little to bolster the interpretation that applicants must

use county tax rolls that are current the date of filing. The phrase “on the date it files an application”

modifies the verb “mail,” while the phrase “as stated on the current county tax rolls” identifies the

source of land ownership information. Notably, there is no rule language linking the word

“current” to the filing date of the application. Moreover, by requiring applicants to deliver notice

“on the date it files an application,” the rule proves that the Commission knows how to establish

specific temporal modifiers when it intends to do so.

          Here, however, the Commission did not set a similar “as of” date for the current county tax

rolls. This structure illustrates that “on the date the application was filed” was not intended to

modify “current county tax rolls.” Nevertheless, the PFD concludes that, because the rule (1) is

 unclear about when county tax rolls are current and (2) requires notice to be mailed on the date of

the filing, the county tax rolls must be current “as of” the date of the filing.7 The PFD is silent,

however, as to how the rule’s text justifies this interpretation. Rather, the only logical justification

for the PFD’s interpretation is the unstated premise that county tax rolls are no longer current

unless they were retrieved on the exact date the application was filed. But the text does not support

this interpretation because the rule never uses any “as of” language to connect tax roll information

with the date of application filing.

          The PFD’s interpretation of the rule is also unworkable. Notice of this application was

provided to thousands of landowners.8 Each notice packet had to include the specific items listed

in 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(3)(A)-(C), making each packet nearly 100 pages long.9 It is unreasonable to

expect an applicant to prepare hundreds of thousands of notice documents for mailing in a single

day. In fact, following the PFD’s logic, applicants would be required to repeatedly pull updated

county tax roll data throughout the application preparation process, which may span several days,

to ensure that no ownership changes occurred between initial data collection and the filing date.

Such an interpretation would impose a continual obligation to refresh records and would

effectively prevent applicants from ever having certainty that the information relied on remained

sufficiently current. And, while the PFD’s interpretation may entail a lesser burden for smaller

applications, the compliance obligation becomes impractical for an application that spans fifteen

counties.

           Rather than offering a novel interpretation of 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(3), the Commission

should adhere to its practical reading of the rule without imposing an additional requirement to

identify tax roll owners on the day of filing. Indeed, despite processing and approving hundreds of

transmission line CCN applications over the years, Staff is not aware of the Commission ever

construing this notice rule as imposing such a strict temporal requirement. Staff therefore contends

that the Applicants satisfied the notice requirements of 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(3).

          Public Meeting Notice under 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4)

          Commission Rule 22.52(a)(4) requires an applicant, at a minimum, “to hold at least one

public meeting prior to the filing of its [application] if 25 or more persons would be entitled to

receive direct mail notice of the application.” According to the PFD, the Applicants’ three public

meetings did not satisfy the public meeting notice requirements of this rule.10 Staff disagrees.

          The PFD applies a new interpretation of the public meeting requirement that is inconsistent

with Commission precedent. The PFD recommends a construction of the rule that would require a

new public meeting if an applicant adds proposed routes after an initial public meeting.11 The

Commission, however, has routinely found that applicants satisfy the public meeting notice

requirements by sending notice to the relevant landowners, “even where the utility subsequently

added or modified links after the public meeting.”12

           Most recently, in Docket No. 59315, Oncor added and modified route links after it had

already held three public meetings.13 Nevertheless, consistent with its prior precedent, the

Commission found that Oncor satisfied the requirements of 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4) by “holding at

least one public meeting and mailing notice of that meeting to landowners within 500 feet of the

centerline of the transmission facilities as the project existed at the time notice was sent.”14 Here,

the Applicants held at least one public meeting after mailing notice of that meeting to landowners

affected by the project as it existed at the time notice was sent. And although the Applicants added

and modified route links after the public meetings, the Applicants should be treated consistently

with Oncor in Docket No. 59315 and found to have satisfied the notice requirement under 16 TAC

§ 22.52(a)(4).

          Ultimately, the Commission “cannot hold a utility responsible for not taking actions that

go beyond what is required in a statute or rule.”15 The Legislature notably did not impose any

public notice meeting requirements in PURA and the current notice rule only requires an applicant

to hold one public meeting after mailing notice. Staff therefore contends that the Applicants

satisfied the public meeting notice requirements of 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4) by holding at least one

public meeting after mailing notice to landowners affected by the project as it existed at the time

notice was sent.

                          III.       EXCEPTIONS TO DETERMINATION OF NEED

          Staff disagrees with the PFD’s conclusions that (1) the Applicants failed to establish that

the projects that comprise Import Path 2 are necessary and (2) ERCOT’s recommendations on the

765-kV import paths are not entitled to great weight.16 Instead, based on the Commission’s recent

consideration of ERCOT’s recommendations for Import Path 1, as well as ERCOT’s broader

transmission planning after the Commission’s approval of the Permian Basin Reliability Plan

(PBRP), great weight should be afforded to ERCOT’s recommendation that the 765-kV import

paths, including Import Path 2, are needed.

          Recent Commission Consideration of the PBRP

          When considering the necessity of Import Path 1 in Docket Nos. 59029 and 59315, the

Commission determined that “[t]he PBRP establishes a need for additional service in the Permian

Basin region to serve existing and projected electrical loads, and [that] the Commission has

identified Import Path 1, which includes the proposed transmission facilities, as part of the solution

to meet that need.”17 In turn, not only did the Commission give great weight to ERCOT’s

determination that Import Path 1 is needed, the Commission more broadly determined that the

PBRP itself establishes the needs for the Permian Basin Region as a whole. In Docket No. 59315,

the Commission concluded that Import Path 1 is only part of solution to meet such needs.

Accordingly, it is only logical to conclude that ERCOT’s recommendation that Import Path 2 is

another part of the solution needed to meet such needs. ERCOT’s recommendations on Import

Path 2 should similarly be entitled to great weight.

           In contrast, the PFD improperly concludes that (1) ERCOT’s recommendations should not

be granted great weight, (2) the preponderance of the evidence outweighs ERCOT’s

recommendation, and (3) the Applicants failed to demonstrate need.18 For the reasons discussed in

Staff’s and the Applicants’ initial and reply briefs, Staff contends that the PFD’s conclusions are

flawed because they fail to afford ERCOT’s broader transmission planning recommendations the

great weight to which they are entitled.19 Instead, based on ERCOT’s recommendations and the

Commission’s recent approval of Import Path 1,20 Staff contends that the two 765-kV transmission

line projects comprising Import Path 2 are necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience,

or safety of the public under PURA § 37.056(a).

          To support its flawed conclusions, the PFD relies on several facts in a manner that (1)

undermines the special status afforded to ERCOT’s recommendations, (2) misconstrues Staff’s

overall position on the need for the projects, and (3) misinterprets ERCOT’s broader transmission

planning recommendations.

import paths or ERCOT’s subsequent recommendation that the import paths are also needed to

help exit the North-to-Far-West and South-to-Far-West Import Generic Transmission Constraints

(Far-West GTCs).21 To the extent that ERCOT’s lack of testimony for these projects informed the

          Third, the PFD misinterprets the significance of ERCOT’s recommendation that the 765-

kV import paths are an upgrade needed to help exit the Far-West GTCs.25 Instead of addressing

this recommendation on its merits separate from ERCOT’s prior PBRP recommendations, the PFD

resolve the deficiencies the PFD claims exist with the load projections in the PBRP.26

          The PFD, however, disregards that ERCOT has not deviated from or re-evaluated its

determination that the PBRP 765-kV import paths remain necessary since initially recommending

those import paths.27 Instead, ERCOT’s recommendation has been consistently reaffirmed through

its broader transmission planning efforts, which are premised on the Commission’s approval for

765-kV import paths.28 Furthermore, ERCOT’s overall recommendation has remained consistent,

despite changing circumstances. As such, the PFD’s assertion that changed circumstances

demonstrates a need to re-evaluate the PBRP and the need for the 765-kV import paths is without

merit.29

                     IV.        EXCEPTIONS TO THE SELECTION OF ROUTE 894

          Staff disagrees with the PFD’s recommendation to select Route 894 over Route 487. Staff

continues to support approval of Route 487 as the route that best meets the governing criteria under

PURA § 37.056 and 16 TAC § 25.101 when compared to Route 894 and other proposed routes.

Route 487 is a reasonable and balanced route that exhibits good quantitative outcomes, while also

providing qualitative benefits consistent with the community values expressed by parties and

residents.32

proceeding: Routes 894, 487, 392, and 296 (focus routes).33 The PFD notes that “[t]he ALJs are

But the PFD does not consider all the routing factors when recommending Route 894 over Route

recreational areas.”37 The PFD then notes, “[c]onversely, no part of Route 894’s centerline runs
